title: The big lookout
hookLine: from a carpenter's town to Rome, from a seed to a creed: look back at the hill you've climbed

lines: HOURS OF LOOKING DOWN AT BOOTS.
THE PATH OPENS ONTO A LEDGE.
cards: On a long trail there's a moment hikers talk about. Hours of looking down at boots: the next rock, the next root. Then the path opens onto a ledge, and you turn around.
There it all is. The parking lot, tiny. The river you crossed.
The steep bit that nearly made you quit. All of it, walked one step at a time. On day one you started at the bottom of this hill with one shared meal.
Today is that ledge: skopos, the mark, and a look back at the whole climb before the path goes on.

teach.b: Camp one was first words. Amen, a word you'd said a thousand times. Grace, a gift you didn't earn.
The Lord's Prayer, one line a day: our Father, thy kingdom come, daily bread, forgive us, deliver us. Agape. The cross.
Easter morning, and the women at the tomb first.

Camp two was the stories: a sower flinging seed on every kind of ground, a father running down the road, a girl in Nazareth, a small carpenter's town, a road through Galilee, a last week in Jerusalem, then Acts, carrying the story to a shipwreck and to Rome.

teach.h: CAMPS TWO AND THREE: STORIES, PRACTICES.
teach.b: Camp three was the practices: ways to pray, Advent candles and the circle of the year, Sabbath, singing, giving, the sacraments, a rule of life.
Camp four was Mark, read in order, breathless, from the first line to the empty tomb and the young man's words: he's going ahead of you to Galilee.

teach.h: CAMP FIVE: THE DEPTHS, AND ROMANS.
teach.b: Camp five went deep: the Sermon on the Mount, the mystics, the whole family of churches, the creeds that grew from that seed, and lately, Paul's letter to Rome. From a mustard seed to a creed.

From prison, Paul wrote to his friends in Philippi, in the King James Bible: "forgetting those things which are behind, and reaching forth unto those things which are before, I press toward the mark." The mark.
The target. Remember hamartia, the word for sin that some readers hear as missing the mark? Paul's answer: don't stop aiming; keep pressing on.
That's where year two begins: the whole Bible, in order, from its first line.

how: Some Christians mark the end of a season or a year by looking back, giving thanks for what has passed before setting out again; in the Ignatian tradition a daily version of this is called the examen.

games.q: you're Paul, writing from prison to friends in Philippi. you look back on everything. what do you say?
o: I've arrived; there's nothing left to climb.
forgetting what's behind, I press toward the mark.
I wish I'd taken an easier road.
games.why: "forgetting those things which are behind, and reaching forth unto those things which are before, I press toward the mark." the hill goes on.

practice: Let the year pass in front of you like the view from the lookout, and find the line that stayed: one of the carries, like fear buries things, the story keeps going, no, not even that; a verse; or something you realized on your own, on an ordinary Tuesday.
Not the most impressive one; the one that's actually yours. If you pray, give thanks for the climb so far.

wordCard.voice: Skopos. Paul's Greek word for the mark, the goal you keep your eyes on, pressing on past what's behind.

orig.note: Greek: the mark, the goal you keep your eyes on.

carryVoice: Your line: the hill goes on. You've walked every step of it. Day three hundred thirty-one.
